name: Log Skeleton
author: István Koren
description: The facts a log never broke: which activities always follow which, which never occur together, which occur equally often, and how many times each may occur in a case. A log skeleton is not a model you walk through — it is a classifier, and it won the Process Discovery Contest by deciding whether a trace belongs rather than by drawing a diagram. Discover one from a log, then check any other log against it.

actions.label: Discover log skeleton
actions.description: Records every fact that held in the log: equivalence (two activities occur equally often), always-before and always-after (ordering at any distance), never-together, directly-follows, and the set of occurrence counts each activity was seen with. With no noise allowed, a fact is kept only if not one case broke it — which is what makes the result usable as a classifier rather than a summary.

agent.whenToUse: To state what a log always does without committing to an order of work, and to get a model that can judge whether a new case belongs.
agent.notFor: Drawing a process. There is nothing to walk through and no notion of a path; use a miner for that.
examples: the defaults (no noise) for the paper's own setting
noise 0.05 on a real-life log, where a handful of cases break everything

noise.title: Noise allowed
noise.description: The share of cases that may break a fact and still leave it in the skeleton. 0 is the paper's own setting: a fact held by every single case. Raising it lets a rule through that a handful of exceptional cases break — and drops the rarest occurrence counts, so one freak case cannot widen the model.

counts.title: How often each activity happens
counts.description: Records the set of occurrence counts each activity was seen with. This is the part with the most classifying power and the part a reader can check against what they know about the process.

equivalence.title: Equivalence
equivalence.description: Two activities that always occur the same number of times. Nothing in DECLARE or in an imperative model says this.

alwaysBefore.title: Always before
alwaysBefore.description: One activity never happens before another has happened.

alwaysAfter.title: Always after
alwaysAfter.description: One activity is always followed by another later in the case.

neverTogether.title: Never together
neverTogether.description: Two activities that never both occur in one case.

directlyFollows.title: Directly follows
directlyFollows.description: One activity is always immediately followed by another, with nothing in between.

limit.title: Most facts to keep
limit.description: A cap on the skeleton's size. What was cut is reported rather than silently dropped.

maxActivities.title: Activity limit
maxActivities.description: Keeps only the most frequent activities. Every ordered pair is a candidate for five relations, so the work grows with the square of this.

actions.label: Classify against a skeleton
actions.description: Decides, case by case, whether a log fits a skeleton: which facts each case broke, and which facts the log breaks most often. This is what the skeleton is for — there is no alignment, no cost and no search, only a fact and the cases that broke it.

agent.whenToUse: To test a skeleton from one period, site or system against another, or to find the cases in a log that do not behave like the rest.
agent.notFor: Scoring an imperative model — use conformance checking (alignments) for a Petri net.

maxCases.title: Cases to list
maxCases.description: How many non-fitting cases to name, worst first. The counts are over the whole log whatever this is set to.

maxActivities.title: Activity limit
maxActivities.description: Keeps only the most frequent activities. A fact about an activity outside the limit is reported as naming an activity this log does not record, rather than silently passing.

authors.name: István Koren
authors.affiliation: ELTE University Budapest, Data Science and Engineering

citation.text: Verbeek, H.M.W. and de Carvalho, R.M. (2018). Log skeletons: a classification approach to process discovery. arXiv:1806.08247. The four ordering relations are evaluated by the DECLARE plugin's crate, which implements the same semantics under their DECLARE names.
